text: Unit 1 – Introduction & Computer System Organization

subject: UNKNOWN
text: Operating Systems (OS) form the backbone of modern computing systems. Every application program, from a simple calculator to complex AI software, relies on the operating system to interact with the hardware. Without an operating system, application developers would need to write hardware-specific code, making software development extremely complex and impractical.

subject: UNKNOWN
text: If an operating system were not developed, application developers would need to directly interact with hardware components such as the CPU, memory, disk, and I/O devices. This would require detailed knowledge of hardware architecture, device protocols, and low-level instructions. The operating system abstracts hardware complexity and provides a standardized interface, allowing developers to focus on solving problems rather than managing hardware.

subject: UNKNOWN
heading_path: General Definition of an Operating System
text: An Operating System is a program that acts as an intermediary between the user and the computer hardware. It provides a user-friendly environment in which users can easily develop and execute programs. Without an operating system: • Hardware knowledge would be mandatory for programming • Software portability would be extremely limited • Resource conflicts would be difficult to manage

subject: UNKNOWN
text: Early computers did not have operating systems. Programs were loaded manually, and only one program could run at a time. Over time, as hardware became more powerful and users demanded multitasking, operating systems evolved to manage resources efficiently and provide better usability.

subject: UNKNOWN
text: Pavan A C (pavanac@pes.edu) 2 Operating System Goals The primary goals of an operating system are: • Execute user programs and make solving user problems easier • Make the computer system convenient to use • Use hardware efficiently • Manage system resources, including: o Memory o Processor(s) o Input/Output devices An effective OS balances user convenience with efficient hardware utilization. Why Study Operating Systems? Although only a small percentage of computer professionals design or modify operating systems, almost all software runs on top of an OS. Understanding operating systems is crucial for: • Writing efficient programs • Developing secure applications

subject: UNKNOWN
text: • Debugging performance issues • Understanding resource behavior such as memory usage and CPU scheduling Knowledge of OS fundamentals leads to proper, efficient, effective, and secure programming. text: Unit 1 – CPU Scheduling CPU Scheduling – Basic Concepts In a computer system with a single CPU core, only one process can execute at a time. All other processes must wait until the CPU becomes free and they are scheduled again. The main objective of multiprogramming is to: • Keep the CPU busy at all times • Maximize CPU utilization To achieve this: • Several processes are kept in main memory • When one process has to wait (usually for I/O), the OS: o Takes the CPU away from that process o Assigns the CPU to another ready process

subject: UNKNOWN
text: This cycle continues, ensuring that the CPU rarely remains idle. CPU Scheduling in Multicore Systems On a multicore system, the same concept is extended: • Each processing core should be kept busy • Scheduling decisions are made independently for each core • Improves overall system throughput and performance CPU Scheduling – Need for Multiprogramming In a simple system without multiprogramming: • A process executes until it must wait (typically for I/O) • During this waiting period, the CPU remains idle • CPU time is wasted and no useful work is done Multiprogramming allows the OS to: • Switch the CPU

subject: UNKNOWN
text: to another ready process • Use waiting time productively This makes CPU scheduling a fundamental OS function. Alternating Sequence of CPU and I/O Bursts Process execution consists of an alternating sequence of CPU bursts and I/O bursts. • CPU burst → process is executing instructions • I/O burst → process is waiting for I/O completion Maximum CPU utilization is achieved when:

Histogram of CPU-Burst Times The duration of CPU bursts: • Varies widely among processes • Follows a characteristic frequency distribution Observations • I/O-bound processes o Many short CPU bursts • CPU-bound processes o Few long CPU bursts This distribution is

Preemptive Scheduling CPU scheduling decisions can occur when a process: 1. Switches from running → waiting 2. Switches from running → ready 3. Switches from waiting → ready 4. text: Unit 1 – Process Concept (Process Management) Process Concept An operating system executes a variety of programs: • Batch systems → execute jobs • Time-shared systems → execute user programs or tasks In operating-system literature, the terms job and process are often used interchangeably. Process vs Program • A program is a passive entity o Stored on disk as an executable file • A process is an active entity o A program in execution A program becomes a process when: • Its executable file is loaded into memory • Execution begins (via GUI click, command line, script, etc.) One program
